acv.quote: Two hundred and ten K ACV.

header.scope: Won: online membership billing only; front desks still on Global Payments, phase two has no date
header.tag_why: The contract sat with the controller for two weeks and was signed four days after Tobi showed which of the customer's own failed renewals were recoverable, so the deciding question was what recovery was worth in their numbers, set against the cost of leaving the incumbent.

evidence.excerpt: They report member churn to the board every quarter, it had ticked up two quarters running
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: somebody finally split it into people who cancelled and people whose card just failed.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: members who never meant to leave.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: I want to say a third of the churn? Don't quote me. It was in her board deck.
evidence.label: opinion

trigger.insight: This was a board-level churn problem before anyone called it a payments problem. Failed payments only came into view when someone split the churn number. The size of the failed-card bucket is unconfirmed: the rep's figure is hedged, and the real number sits in Maya's board deck, which we apparently never saw.
trigger.messaging: Pitch M10 as recovering involuntary churn, using 'members who never meant to leave' framing, instead of as a smart-retries feature.

evidence.excerpt: She said it was her call.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: The paper had gone to Greg and it sat with him for two weeks.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: His signature's on it.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Maya chose us. Greg decided whether anybody got chosen.
evidence.label: opinion

decider.insight: The rep's first answer rested on Maya's own claim that it was her call. The facts show a second gate: the controller held the paper and signed it. Maya picked the vendor, but Greg decided whether switching happened at all. Greg said nothing until he saw money in their own file, and the only other question on record from him was about termination fees.
decider.messaging: Build a controller-ready version of the recovery case: recoverable revenue from their own failed renewals, set against exit and switching costs. Put it in front of finance before the contract reaches them.

evidence.excerpt: they came back with a rate review and a new terminal bundle for the front desks, on a longer contract.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: I didn't see any of it. That's her telling me.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: After it was, what readers do you have, do they work inside our studio software, what's the contract term, what does it cost to get out.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Greg asked about termination fees twice.
evidence.label: fact

competitor.insight: The incumbent did not fight on failed payments. Per Maya, it moved the conversation to front-desk hardware and contract length, where it is already embedded through the studio software, and the customer's questions followed straight away. The counteroffer is known only secondhand, and the rep's view that the incumbent was rattled is his own read.
competitor.messaging: Expect the incumbent to counter with a hardware bundle. Come with a staged-switch answer (memberships first, front desk later) and clear answers on term and exit cost, so the deal isn't fought on their ground.

evidence.excerpt: Tobi, took an export of one month of their failed renewals and showed which ones were the kind that usually come back with a retry or an updated card.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Their file, not our average.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: I opened with the global slide. They have studios in the US and a handful in Canada.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: is that the readers?
evidence.label: quote

message.insight: The pitch that landed was not M10 or M6 as written. It was a diagnosis of the customer's own data, the opposite of an average-uplift or independent-study claim. M1's global opener got silence from a business with studios in the US and a handful in Canada. M3's 'unified commerce' meant nothing to Maya until she translated it into hardware.
message.messaging: Open with an analysis of their own failed-renewal export instead of the global slide, and replace 'unified commerce' with concrete words like readers at the front desk.

evidence.excerpt: Before that I honestly thought we were there to keep the incumbent honest.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: Greg hadn't said a word in two meetings, and he asked for the spreadsheet.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Then we did the data session, and four days later it was signed.
evidence.label: fact

decided.insight: The turning point was the data session, not a negotiation: two weeks of nothing, then a signature four days after the controller asked for the spreadsheet. Until then the rep thought we were a stalking horse. The original pitch alone was not moving the person holding the pen.
decided.messaging: Make the own-data recovery session a standard early step aimed at finance, not a late rescue move.

evidence.excerpt: We couldn't show that live. It runs through a partner integration, and the partner did a call the week after.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: the studio managers will revolt.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: They saw the partner's demo. Not in their own setup.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Not yet. It depends on the partner piece.
evidence.label: fact

gaps.insight: We could not show our reader inside their studio software. The customer saw only a partner demo, not their own setup. That is exactly why the win is memberships-only and the front desks are still on Global with no date. M3's claim that the line between online and in-store has disappeared did not hold up here: in-store depends on a partner and was never proven in their environment.
gaps.messaging: Don't claim unified online and in-store until we can demo the reader inside the customer's own front-desk software. Until then, name the partner integration openly and present memberships as phase one.

evidence.excerpt: members who never meant to leave.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: is that the readers?
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: the studio managers will revolt.
evidence.label: quote

gaps.question: What exact words did they use for their problem?
gaps.follow_up: Ask the rep on Slack for Maya's and Greg's own phrases for failed payments and the front desk. Note that the quotes above surfaced in other answers, not in answer to this question.

gaps.question: How big was the failed-card share of churn?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Maya (via the rep) for the failed-card churn figure from her board deck.

gaps.question: Who made the final call, and how do you know?
gaps.follow_up: Ask the rep what Greg needed to see before signing, and whether he weighed termination fees against the recovery spreadsheet.

gaps.question: What exactly was in the incumbent's counteroffer?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Maya what the rate review and terminal bundle offered, and what contract term was proposed.

gaps.question: When does phase two (front desks) start?
gaps.follow_up: Ask the rep and the partner what the partner integration needs before a date can be set, and whether the customer has a test in their own setup scheduled.

close.rep_takeaway: Find out early who holds the pen, not just who runs the evaluation. Here the controller sat on the paper for two weeks and moved only when he saw recovery in his own company's file. Lead with their data, not the global slide, and get it to finance before the contract does.
